title: The dragon king's daughter (Kern ch. 11)
hook: in this chapter the young naga princess offers a jewel and awakens in an instant, to the disciples' surprise

segments.voice: Yesterday, a jeweled tower hung in the sky, and an ancient Buddha moved over to make room. Your line: two on one seat. Who did you sit beside? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-six.

Someone in the middle of chapter eleven says, out loud, that he doesn't believe it. Not a scoffer in the back row. A bodhisattva named Prajnakuta, the attendant who came with the Buddha of the jeweled tower. He's just been told that a young girl, the daughter of the dragon king who rules under the sea, has reached the very edge of awakening. He knows how long the road is supposed to take. Ages. Lifetimes. Countless gifts and sacrifices. A child, from the ocean, from a family of serpents? No. Then she walks in. Today: the dragon king's daughter.
screen: `HE DOESN'T BELIEVE IT.` → `A GIRL FROM UNDER THE SEA.` → `THEN SHE WALKS IN.`

segments.voice: First, the setup. The bodhisattva Manjushri rises up out of the ocean, where he's been teaching the Lotus in the palace of Sagara, the naga king. Nagas are serpent beings of the waters; English often calls them dragons. Prajnakuta asks him: has anyone there taken this teaching in deeply enough to awaken quickly? Manjushri says yes: Sagara's young daughter. Wise, kind, steady in meditation. Second, the doubt. Prajnakuta says the Buddha himself strove for ages before awakening. He can't believe a girl could do it in a moment. Then the girl appears, bows, and praises the Buddha. And the senior disciple Sariputra adds his own objection: a woman's body, he says, cannot reach buddhahood. Third, the jewel. She holds a jewel of enormous worth, and she offers it to the Buddha. He accepts it at once. She turns to the two doubters: was that quick? Very quick, they say. Watch me, she says, awaken faster than that. Fourth, the instant. In front of the whole assembly, the text shows her form changing to a male one, and she appears in a world to the south, seated under a bodhi tree, fully awake, teaching. Prajnakuta and Sariputra go silent. That change of body is read in more than one way. Some readers hear in it the old assumption that a woman must first become a man. Others point out that she awakens anyway, faster than the objection can finish, and hear the objection answered. The chapter itself ends with two senior figures silent, and a young girl teaching.
screen: `MANJUSHRI COMES UP FROM THE SEA.` · `I DON'T BELIEVE IT.` · `A JEWEL, ACCEPTED AT ONCE.` · `FASTER THAN THE OBJECTION.` · then, large: `IN AN INSTANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: don't underestimate someone young. Settle, and let the breath come and go. Bring to mind one young person you know: a niece, a student, a new hire, a kid down the street. Remember something they said or did that you brushed off, or didn't take seriously. Now hold, for a few breaths, the real possibility that they saw something you didn't. Let the doubt go quiet, the way Prajnakuta's did. Then let the picture go, and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The dragon king's daughter. A young naga girl, doubted by two senior figures, offers a jewel and awakens in front of everyone. Today's word.
Your line: in an instant. Today, ask someone younger than you a real question, and let their answer change your mind if it can. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, the naga king's daughter is remembered as the girl who awakened in an instant, and traditions read the change of her body in different ways.

fork.setup: you're the naga king's daughter. two senior figures have just said, in front of everyone, that you can't do this. what do you do?

offer your jewel, then awaken in front of them.
fork.reveal: she offers a jewel, the Buddha accepts it at once, and she awakens faster than that. the doubters go silent.

original.note: Sanskrit: a serpent being of the waters, often called a dragon in English; the dragon king's people.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fairy tale about a dragon princess.
what it means: a young naga girl, doubted by two senior figures, offers a jewel and awakens in front of the whole assembly.
what a scholar hears: the scene answers Sariputra's objection about women's bodies, and readers have taken her change of body both as a limit and as a rebuttal.

sources.ref: Saddharma-pundarika, ch. 11 (Kern's numbering; ch. 12 in Kumarajiva's Chinese)

notes: Scene paraphrased from Kern (1884) ch. 11, not quoted (wording unverified). Kern keeps this episode inside ch. 11; Kumarajiva's Chinese has it in the separate Devadatta chapter (12). The source ref says so; confirm.
The girl's age is given in the text (commonly eight); deliberately left out under the claims rule. Restore if a Keeper wants it.

Check order: Prajnakuta's doubt, the girl appears and praises, Sariputra's objection (the five ranks a woman cannot attain), jewel offered and accepted, 'was that quick?', transformation, awakening in the southern world (Vimala), silence of Prajnakuta and Sariputra.

The gender transformation is handled by naming readings without ranking: as an old limit, and as the objection answered. 'Some Buddhist women have held her up as their own' is a general reception claim; confirm or soften. Sensitive: a Keeper should read this paragraph closely.

Editor: hook's quoted 'I don't believe it' recast as paraphrase (not exact public-domain wording); cut the sweeping 'by the rules everyone assumed in that world', 'through the centuries', the unsourced 'some Buddhist women have held her up' line, and the superlative 'the youngest person present'.
